name: Mass–Energy Equivalence
what: This subtopic covers Einstein's relationship between mass and energy: E₀ = mc², total relativistic energy Etot = γmc², and relativistic kinetic energy Ek = (γ − 1)mc². It applies these to nuclear fusion, positron–electron annihilation, and nuclear transmutation in particle accelerators.
why: Mass–energy equivalence is one of the most profound results of special relativity. It explains how the Sun produces energy, how PET scans work, and how particle accelerators can create new particles. It also demonstrates that the classical kinetic energy formula ½mv² fails at high speeds.

items.title: I can apply E₀ = mc² to convert between rest mass and rest energy
items.what: The rest energy E₀ of an object is the energy equivalent of its mass when it is stationary. Even at rest, every object with mass has enormous energy stored within it, given by E₀ = mc².
items.why: This is the foundational formula of mass–energy equivalence and is used in all calculations involving mass conversion to energy, including nuclear fusion and annihilation.
items.example: An electron has a rest mass of 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg. Its rest energy is E₀ = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J = 0.511 MeV.

items.title: I can calculate total relativistic energy using Etot = γmc²
items.what: The total energy of a moving object is Etot = γmc², where γ is the Lorentz factor. This includes both the rest energy E₀ = mc² and the relativistic kinetic energy. As v → c, Etot → ∞.
items.why: Total energy is conserved in all physical processes. This formula is needed for any calculation involving the energy of a relativistic particle, including those in particle accelerators.
items.example: A proton (m = 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ kg) moving at 0.999c (γ = 22.4) has total energy Etot = 22.4 × 1.67 × 10⁻²⁷ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 3.36 × 10⁻⁹ J.

items.title: I can calculate relativistic kinetic energy using Ek = (γ − 1)mc²
items.what: Relativistic kinetic energy is the total energy minus the rest energy: Ek = (γ − 1)mc². At low speeds this approximates the classical ½mv², but at relativistic speeds it is significantly larger and approaches infinity as v approaches c.
items.why: The classical formula ½mv² fails for particles moving near the speed of light. Using it for particles in accelerators gives serious errors. The relativistic formula shows why particles cannot be accelerated to the speed of light — the energy required becomes infinite.

items.title: I can apply ΔE = Δmc² to calculate energy released in nuclear fusion
items.what: In nuclear fusion, lighter nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus. The products have slightly less mass than the reactants — this mass defect Δm is converted to energy according to ΔE = Δmc².
items.why: Nuclear fusion is the energy source of the Sun and stars. Understanding mass defect and energy release from E = Δmc² is a direct application of Einstein's formula to real physical processes.

items.title: I can apply ΔE = Δmc² to calculate energy released in positron–electron annihilation
items.what: When a positron and electron meet, they annihilate completely, converting all of their combined rest mass into energy in the form of two gamma rays emitted in opposite directions. Each gamma ray carries energy equal to the rest energy of one electron.
items.why: Positron–electron annihilation is a direct and complete conversion of mass to energy. It is also the physical basis of PET scans used in medical imaging.
items.example: Each gamma ray has energy E = mc² = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ J = 0.511 MeV. Total energy released = 2 × 8.20 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 1.64 × 10⁻¹³ J.

items.title: I can apply ΔE = Δmc² to nuclear transmutation in particle accelerators
items.what: When particles collide at high speed in an accelerator, nuclei can be broken apart and rearranged, producing different elements — this is nuclear transmutation. The mass difference between reactants and products is accounted for by the energy released or absorbed in the collision.
items.why: Particle accelerators are used to study nuclear structure and create new elements. The mass–energy relationship is what makes it possible to predict and quantify the energy involved in these collisions.
items.example: In a collision, reactants have combined mass 3.67 × 10⁻²⁵ kg and products have mass 3.60 × 10⁻²⁵ kg. Mass defect Δm = 0.07 × 10⁻²⁵ kg. Energy released: ΔE = 0.07 × 10⁻²⁵ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² = 6.30 × 10⁻¹⁰ J.

items.title: I can interpret a graph of Lorentz factor (γ) vs relative speed and explain its implications for energy and mass
items.what: The Lorentz factor γ starts at 1 when v = 0 and increases gradually, then steeply, approaching infinity as v approaches c. This means total energy and kinetic energy both approach infinity as speed approaches c.
items.why: This graph shows visually why it is impossible to accelerate a massive object to the speed of light — infinite energy would be required. It also explains why relativistic effects are negligible at everyday speeds.
items.example: At v = 0.1c, γ ≈ 1.005 — barely any effect. At v = 0.9c, γ ≈ 2.29. At v = 0.99c, γ ≈ 7.09. At v = 0.999c, γ ≈ 22.4. The curve rises steeply near v = c.
